lesson.title: Sequence Is Destiny: Reading a Protein's First Draft
lesson.summary: Primary structure is the specific, linear order of amino acids in a polypeptide chain, and because that order is set by peptide bonds running from the N-terminus to the C-terminus, it is the foundation that determines every higher level of a protein's three-dimensional shape.
lesson.body:
Primary structure is the simplest way to describe a protein: it is just the order of amino acids, written out from the N-terminus to the C-terminus, connected one after another by peptide bonds. Nothing about primary structure involves folding or three-dimensional shape yet, it is purely a sequence, similar to reading letters in a word from left to right. A short chain of a few amino acids is called a peptide, a longer chain is a polypeptide, and a functional polypeptide, or a set of polypeptides working together, is what we generally call a protein.

That sequence is not chosen at random. It is specified by the sequence of a gene and is assembled during translation according to the genetic code, so ultimately the order of amino acids in a protein traces back to the order of nucleotides in DNA. This is why primary structure matters so much: it is the direct output of genetic information, and any error introduced at the DNA level, a mutation, can show up as a change in this sequence.

The consequences of a changed sequence can be dramatic even when only one amino acid out of hundreds is affected. Sickle cell anemia, discussed earlier in the context of amino acid side chains, is fundamentally a primary structure problem: a single DNA base change alters one codon, which swaps the glutamate normally found at position six of the hemoglobin beta chain for a valine. That one substitution is enough to change how the whole protein behaves. This is the central lesson of primary structure, small changes in sequence can produce large changes in function, because sequence controls folding, and folding controls what a protein can do.

Primary structure was also historically the first level of protein architecture that scientists were able to fully determine. In the early 1950s, Frederick Sanger worked out the complete amino acid sequence of insulin, showing that it is not one continuous chain but two separate polypeptides, an A chain of twenty-one amino acids and a B chain of thirty, held together by covalent disulfide bonds between cysteine residues. That achievement proved that proteins have an exact, reproducible sequence rather than some vague or variable composition, and it opened the door to understanding how sequence relates to shape and function.

Primary structure is held together exclusively by the covalent peptide bonds described earlier, which makes it strong and stable compared to what comes next. Every higher level of protein architecture, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structure, is built on top of this sequence and is stabilized by weaker, noncovalent interactions among the amino acid side chains. In other words, primary structure is the fixed instruction set, and everything about how a protein actually folds in three dimensions follows from it.
